rationale: B wins by asking the proof questions that would save a founder from walking into the inbox half-dressed: "if the results ran months ago, the peg is the launch and the profit is context" is exactly the timing problem A misses. A has the cleaner third story in "A 9-million-customer UK bank tests whether its home playbook survives America," but it weakens itself with "then spent it on a second shot at America," which smuggles in funding causality. B still has a forced "exec-spotlight" angle, but its proof discipline is sharper where the pitch would actually break.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo posted its first annual profit — then spent it on a second shot at America" overclaims causality; the update gives sequence, not evidence that profit funded the US launch.
"The first pre-tax profit and the US launch landed in the same year" misses the publication-date problem; if the profit news ran months earlier, it is context, not a fresh peg.
"how the US entry playbook has changed" gestures at a broader trend without supplied evidence beyond Monzo's own partner-bank route.
"Any same-day news-peg angle" is too broad as a refusal; the launch itself is the peg, even if no external breaking hook was supplied.
gaps_in_B: "Monzo's first profitable year is paying for a second shot at America" is causal language the facts do not support; asking for funding proof later does not erase the overpromise.
"Story type: exec-spotlight" is forced without a named executive in the update; this is a rollout-mechanics angle pretending it already has a protagonist.
"Reporters who covered the first failure have a built-in reason" assumes prior coverage and a usable follow-up audience not supplied in the update.
"what it costs in control and margin" may be a smart reporter question, but it imports economics the supplied facts do not establish.
